question: ATS-2025 Table 100.6.3, sinusoidal VLF acceptance test for a 15 kV cable system, phase-to-ground, is:
choices: 21 kV rms for at least 30 minutes
explanation: The acceptance row is 21 kV rms, and the notes call for a minimum of 30 minutes (60 if the circuit is critical). 16 kV is the MTS-2023 maintenance value for 15 kV, not the ATS acceptance value. 56 kV DC is the extruded-dielectric DC table, which is a different test.

question: Table 100.6.6's worked note: Uo for a new 15 kV cable is:
explanation: Uo is phase-to-ground. 15 / √3 = 8.7 kV. 21 kV is the acceptance VLF withstand, not Uo. Tan-delta steps are 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 times Uo.

question: Charging current of a cable is proportional to frequency. Moving a withstand from 60 Hz to 0.1 Hz changes that current by about:
explanation: I = 2πfCV, so the ratio of frequencies is 60 / 0.1 = 600. That is why a VLF set can energize a long cable a 60 Hz set cannot. The voltage and the hold time still have to be the table values.

question: A 15 kV shielded cable. Which VLF rms phase-to-ground voltages match ATS acceptance and MTS maintenance?
explanation: ATS-2025 Table 100.6.3 acceptance for 15 kV is 21 kV rms. MTS-2023 Table 100.6.3 maintenance for 15 kV is 16 kV rms. Both notes use a 30-minute minimum. 8.7 kV is Uo for a 15 kV system, not the withstand.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.6.3; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.6.3

question: ATS Table 100.6.1, extruded dielectric shielded cable, note 2 says:
choices: DC testing is preferred after 5 years because it is gentler
After 5 years of service, DC testing is not recommended
DC testing is forbidden on all new cable
explanation: The note says after 5 years of service, DC testing is not recommended. New cable still has a DC column in that table, with a 15-minute hold, but service-aged extruded cable is not where you reach for DC first. VLF is the separate table.

question: PE-insulated cable, VLF tan delta, sinusoidal 0.1 Hz. Table 100.6.7.1 says tip-up (1.5 Uo minus 0.5 Uo) requires action when it is:
explanation: Acceptable tip-up is below 5 (in units of 10⁻³), further study is 5 to 80, and action required is above 80. If any one of standard deviation, tip-up, or mean lands in a worse column, the cable takes that worse grade. EPR uses Table 100.6.7.2, not this one.

question: ATS Table 100.6.3 sinusoidal acceptance voltage for a 5 kV shielded cable, phase to ground, is:
explanation: The 5 kV row is 10 kV rms. 21 kV is the 15 kV row. The notes still want at least 30 minutes, and a cosine-rectangular waveform is the rms value times √2.

question: For a cosine-rectangular VLF set, ATS Table 100.6.3 says to take the sinusoidal rms value and:
explanation: The note says cosine-rectangular waveforms use the table voltage times the square root of 2. Using the sine number on a cosine-rectangular set undervoltages the cable.

question: PE-insulated cable, tan delta in units of 10⁻³. A mean value that requires action under Table 100.6.7.1 is:
explanation: Mean at a step: acceptable below 4, further study from 4 to 50, action required above 50. Tip-up has its own 5 and 80 limits. One bad column sets the grade.

question: An EPR cable’s tan-delta mean is 40 × 10⁻³. Using Table 100.6.7.2, that result is:
choices: Acceptable, because PE’s action line is 50
Further study (35 to 120), not yet action-required
Action required, because PE’s acceptable line is 4
Invalid, because EPR uses the PE table
explanation: EPR’s own table: mean acceptable below 35, further study from 35 to 120, action required above 120. Grading EPR with the PE mean of 4 condemns a cable the EPR table still calls further study. Fill type can move the EPR numbers; unknown fill uses this table.

question: ATS Table 100.6.3 acceptance voltage for a 25 kV shielded cable, sinusoidal, phase to ground, is:
explanation: The 25 kV row is 32 kV rms. 16 kV is the MTS maintenance value for 15 kV, not this acceptance row. Hold at least 30 minutes unless the note’s 60-minute case applies.

question: Choosing a megohmmeter voltage for a 600 V cable when the manufacturer is silent means:
choices: The highest range on the set, to be sure
The Table 100.1 test voltage for that rating, 1000 V DC, not a 5 kV or 10 kV shot
explanation: Table 100.1 for a 600 V rating is a 1000 V DC test. The meter’s top range is not the specimen’s rating. A voltage lock on the set is how you keep from exceeding the voltage you actually chose.

question: Why is VLF often used instead of dc for field withstand testing of shielded extruded cable?
choices: DC hipot is gentler on aged XLPE
Charging current falls with frequency, so a portable set can energize a long cable
0.1 Hz raises the voltage stress on purpose above the BIL
Tan delta cannot be measured at 0.1 Hz
explanation: The 400.2-2024 introduction, which is not a numbered requirement of the standard, explains that charging current at 0.1 Hz is on the order of 1/600 of the 60 Hz value, so a portable set can energize a long shielded cable. ATS Table 100.6.3 is the acceptance voltage adapted from that guide, and the table’s DC note discourages DC on extruded cable after years in service.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.3.3.B.5.2 and Table 100.6.3; ref. IEEE 400.2-2024 introduction (charging current at 0.1 Hz)

question: When the manufacturer is silent, ATS 7.3.3.B.4 sets the one-minute jacket test at:
choices: At least 2 kV up to 35 kV cable, and at least 5 kV above 35 kV
The same voltage as the VLF withstand
explanation: The jacket test is not the insulation withstand. Up through 35 kV the floor in that sentence is 2 kV; above 35 kV it is 5 kV. Manufacturer data still wins when it exists.

question: ATS 7.3.3.D.2 says to investigate a cable shield whose resistance is:
explanation: The shield has to be continuous. More than 10 ohms per 1000 feet is the investigate line. A shield that reads open will not do its job for the withstand or for a ground-fault return.

question: An offline partial-discharge test on shielded cable passes ATS 7.3.3.D.8 when:
choices: Any discharge is present at operating voltage
There is no partial discharge at or below the threshold in the manufacturer’s data or in IEEE 400.3
The jacket ohms are above 10 per foot
The VLF set trips on overcurrent
explanation: Offline PD is judged against the manufacturer’s voltage threshold or IEEE 400.3. A trip of the withstand set is a failure of a different test. Record inception, extinction, location, and the phase pattern rather than a single beep.

question: On an offline PD test of shielded cable per ATS 7.3.3, partial-discharge inception voltage is:
choices: The voltage where repetitive discharges first appear as the voltage is raised
The voltage where discharges stop as the voltage is lowered
explanation: Inception is the first appearance on the way up. Extinction is the cease point on the way down. ATS 7.3.3.B.8 tells you to record both, along with location and magnitude. The withstand voltage is a different test.

question: ATS 7.3.3.D.7, for an online partial-discharge test of shielded cable, expects:
choices: A reported discharge from the cable at operating voltage
No evidence of partial discharge from the cable, with background noise kept out of the report
A turns-ratio test of the splice
explanation: Online, there should be no cable discharge. If something is there, record amplitude, repetition, and the phase pattern so internal, surface, and corona can be told apart. Background noise is not reported as cable PD.

question: A cable dielectric withstand is accepted when:
choices: Leakage current follows one required slope for every cable
No distress or insulation failure is seen by the end of the voltage application
The set trips and is reset once
explanation: The withstand passes when the insulation shows no distress and does not fail by the end of the voltage application. A rising leakage current is a reason to stop and investigate. It is not a slope you must match to call the test good. Discharge the cable before you handle it.

question: After a VLF or other dielectric withstand, the cable passes when:
choices: A fixed number of minutes has elapsed after the voltage is removed
No distress or failure is observed by the end of the voltage application
Leakage current matches one required slope for every insulation
explanation: The withstand is accepted when nothing is in distress and the insulation has not failed by the end of the shot. That acceptance line does not set a wait, in minutes, before the cable is safe to touch. Discharge it and keep the shields grounded until the charge is gone.

question: For cable rated above 1000 V, NFPA 70B-2026 Table 18.3.5 says to select at least one of:
choices: Very-low-frequency below 1 Hz, DC overpotential, AC power factor or dissipation factor, partial discharge, or power frequency
Only a DC megohmmeter, the same rule as cable through 1000 V
explanation: Above 1000 V you choose at least one method from that list. Very-low-frequency in this table means below 1 Hz. Cable rated 1000 V and below is an insulation-resistance test, not that menu. The chapter does not print a pass/fail kilovolt.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 chapter 18 stops cable maintenance at:
choices: The final branch-circuit overcurrent device; conductors downstream of that device are outside this chapter
Every lighting whip in the building
explanation: The chapter stops at the load side of the final branch-circuit overcurrent device. Above 1000 V, what it covers is purpose-built multilayer cable through 69 kV, not every conductor up to that voltage. A branch-circuit whip past the final device is outside the chapter.

question: Which test does NFPA 70B-2026 Table 18.3.5 assign to cable rated 1000 V and below, rather than to the over-1000 V menu?
choices: A required very-low-frequency withstand at a stated kilovolt
explanation: Through 1000 V the cable test in that table is insulation resistance. The very-low-frequency, DC overpotential, power-factor, partial-discharge, and power-frequency choices are the over-1000 V list, and you pick at least one of those. No kilovolt limit is printed.

question: Very-low-frequency testing, as NFPA 70B-2026 Table 18.3.5 uses the term for cable above 1000 V, means a frequency:
choices: 60 Hz, called very low because the voltage is reduced
The same as a DC insulation-resistance test
explanation: The over-1000 V menu includes very-low-frequency below 1 Hz, DC overpotential, AC power factor or dissipation factor, partial discharge, and power frequency. You choose at least one. The table does not print the test voltage. For equipment above 1000 V, the electrical maintenance program is what selects the insulation-test method. The manufacturer and a NETA table are not the only source of that choice.

question: ATS points to a cable-testing guide for VLF withstand and diagnostics. That guide covers:
choices: Field testing shielded cable with very low frequency
explanation: ATS Table 100.6.3 is the acceptance VLF table, adapted from IEEE 400.2-2024, and 7.3.3.B.5.2 is the VLF withstand test. Dissolved gas is IEEE C57.104. Device numbers used on a relay test are the ATS 7.9.1 list, which follows the C37.2 numbering system.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.6.3 and 7.3.3.B.5.2; ref. IEEE 400.2-2024

question: You just finished a 15-minute dc withstand on a paper-insulated lead-covered feeder and grounded it. The crew wants to rerun the test right away. How long should the cable stay grounded first?
choices: At least 60 minutes, four times the previous test
5 minutes is enough once the meter reads zero
No wait is needed if a discharge stick was used
explanation: A dc-tested cable stores charge that keeps coming back out of the insulation after the first discharge. The guidance is to leave it grounded for at least four times the length of the previous test before retesting, so 4 × 15 min = 60 min. Source: IEEE 400.1-2018, 4.3.

question: Your dc test set will take a laminated cable to 56 kV. What is the minimum resistance of the discharge resistor you should use?
explanation: The recommended discharge resistor is at least 5000 Ω per kV of test voltage. 5000 Ω/kV × 56 kV = 280,000 Ω, or 280 kΩ. It must also withstand the full test voltage and the stored energy (½CV²). Source: IEEE 400.1-2018, 3.2.3.

question: During the voltage hold of a dc test on a paper-insulated (laminated) cable, the leakage current starts to climb slowly and then faster, with no change in voltage. This most likely means:
choices: The cable is drying out and will pass
Insulation failure may be developing, so reduce the voltage quickly
explanation: A steady or falling current at constant voltage is the practical pass sign. Current that rises at a growing rate without any voltage change points to an insulation failure in progress, and the voltage should come down fast. Source: IEEE 400.1-2018, 5.1.

question: On a 1.5 km paper-insulated three-phase feeder, the dc test gives insulation resistances (V ÷ I) of 9000, 8000, and 2500 MΩ. What does that suggest?
choices: All phases are fine since each is above 1000 MΩ
The ratio between the best and worst phase is above 3:1, so the low phase is suspect
The test voltage was too low
Long cables always show this spread
explanation: Comparing the three conductors is useful. On cables longer than about 1000 m, a ratio above about 3:1 between phases suggests a problem in the low one. 9000 ÷ 2500 = 3.6. Source: IEEE 400.1-2018, 5.2.

question: A damped ac (DAC) set is used for an offline PD test on a short run of shielded cable. The test frequency comes out above the set's range. Why, and what is the usual fix?
choices: The frequency is set by the cable capacitance with the set's inductor, so a short cable needs added capacitance
The cable is too long, so test a shorter section
Raise the test voltage to lower the frequency
explanation: A DAC set charges the cable and then rings it through an inductor, so the frequency is the natural frequency of that LC circuit. Less capacitance means a higher frequency. To stay in the 20 to 500 Hz range on a short cable, extra capacitive load is added. Source: IEEE 400.4-2015, 5.1 and 6.1.

question: How is the length of a damped ac (DAC) withstand test on cable defined?
choices: In minutes, like a VLF test
By a set number of DAC excitations at the chosen test voltage
By the time until leakage current stabilizes
explanation: A DAC withstand applies a predetermined number of damped excitations, and the test voltage is the peak of the first cycle. That is different from a VLF or dc test, which run for a set number of minutes. Source: IEEE 400.4-2015, 5.1.

question: Per IEEE 48-2020, what separates a Class 1 termination from Class 2 and Class 3?
choices: Class 1 adds a seal against the environment (and holds system pressure, if any) on top of stress control and external insulation
Class 1 is for indoor use only
Class 1 is only for laminated cable
explanation: Class 3 provides only stress control. Class 2 adds external insulation from conductor to ground. Class 1 adds a seal to the cable end and maintains design pressure, if any. Class 1A is for extruded cable, 1B for laminated, and 1C for pressurized systems. Source: IEEE 48-2020, Clause 3 definitions.

question: What does IEEE 48-2020 say about dc voltage tests on terminations after installation?
choices: They are required at 80% of factory dc
They are not recommended and no longer required; old values are kept for reference only in an annex
They are required only on Class 1C
They replace the ac routine test
explanation: Field tests on the installed system are allowed as acceptance or proof tests for all classes, but direct voltage testing is not recommended and is no longer required. Prior dc values are shown in Annex C for reference. Source: IEEE 48-2020, 8.6.

question: For termination voltage tests, IEEE 48-2020 sets the rate of rise. After quickly reaching 75% of test value, how long should it take to reach full test voltage?
explanation: Unless specified otherwise, start at no more than 20% of the test voltage, raise quickly to 75%, then reach the full value in 15 to 30 s. The voltage is held for the time in the tables. Source: IEEE 48-2020, 8.2.3 and 8.2.4.

question: Per IEEE 404-2012, a joint that connects an extruded dielectric cable to a laminated (paper) cable is called:
explanation: IEEE 404 sorts joints as extruded (both cables extruded), laminated (both paper or laminated), and transition (extruded to laminated). Source: IEEE 404-2012, 3.1.

question: Which joint type does IEEE 404-2012 say can receive production electrical testing at the factory?
explanation: Premolded and single-component cold-shrink joints integrate stress control, insulation, and shield during molding, so they can be production tested. Heat-shrink, multi-component cold-shrink, and taped joints are built up in the field and can't be. Source: IEEE 404-2012, 3.2.

question: IEEE 400.1-2018 says the dc test voltage should stay stable within what band during the test?
explanation: Supply variations can cause big swings in the current reading, so the test voltage should stay within 3% during the test time. Source: IEEE 400.1-2018, 3.2.2.

question: A new 15 kV feeder has been pulled, but the splices and terminations aren't made yet. The owner wants a field test now. In cable-testing terms, that is:
explanation: An installation test is run after the cable is installed but before joints or terminations go on. An acceptance test comes after the full cable system, accessories included, is installed but before it goes into service. A maintenance test is done during the operating life. Source: IEEE 400-2023, 3.1.

question: On a 200 A underground system, a lineman plans to pull an elbow under load. Per IEEE 386-2016, which connector type is designed for that?
choices: Any separable connector with a test point
A bushing well with no insert
explanation: A loadbreak connector is designed to close and interrupt rated load current or less on energized circuits, and it also has a fault-close rating. A deadbreak connector may be separated and engaged only on de-energized circuits. Source: IEEE 386-2016, Clause 3.

question: What does a time-domain reflectometer (TDR) on a medium-voltage cable mainly show you?
choices: Whether the insulation will pass a later withstand test
Where impedance changes along the cable
explanation: A TDR sends a low-voltage pulse between conductor and shield and times the reflections from impedance changes. It finds length, splices, opens, shorts, and corroded neutrals. IEEE 400 notes that it usually will not reveal even serious insulation defects. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.3.3.B.3; IEEE 400-2023, 6.5 and Table 12.

question: On a medium-voltage cable system, the NEC 100 percent insulation level may be used when ground faults are cleared:
choices: Only by a fuse, never by a relay
explanation: 100 percent level requires relaying that clears ground faults within 1 minute. When that can't be met but the faulted section is de-energized within 1 hour, the 133 percent level is used. Source: NFPA 70-2023 315.10(C)(1) and (C)(2).

question: On a 200 A loadbreak elbow, the test point is:
choices: A capacitive tap for voltage sensing
A bonding point for the concentric neutral wires
The place to clamp a temporary ground
A port for injecting TDR pulses
explanation: IEEE 386 defines the test point as capacitively coupled to the conductor so a fault indicator or voltage sensor can read through it. It is not a grounding or test-lead connection. Source: IEEE 386-2016, clause 3 (test point).

question: You need to take an elbow-terminated cable off a transformer bushing and keep the cable end insulated on the parking stand. Which accessory do you use?
choices: A reducing tap well with an insulated cap
explanation: An insulated parking bushing mounts on the parking stand and gives the elbow an insulated, shielded place to sit. A bushing well plug and an insulated cap cover an unused bushing or well instead. Source: IEEE 386-2016, clause 3 (insulated parking bushing).

question: A cable has a 30-ohm characteristic impedance. A TDR pulse meets a section of 10 ohms. The reflection coefficient and what the trace shows are:
choices: -1.0: a full inverted reflection, like a dead short
explanation: rho = (Zd - Zo)/(Zd + Zo) = (10 - 30)/(10 + 30) = -0.5. A lower impedance gives a negative reflection, toward the -1 of a dead short. An open is +1. Source: IEEE 400-2023, 6.5.

question: TDR traces on phases A and C show a clean far end at 2,400 ft. Phase B shows the same end plus a strong reflection at 1,150 ft. ATS 7.3.3 says:
choices: Accept it, because the far end shows at the correct length
Accept it if phase B passes insulation resistance
Investigate phase B at 1,150 ft; traces must match
Repeat with a dc hipot to confirm the TDR
explanation: The TDR pass condition is that the trace clearly shows the cable length and matches the other phases. An extra reflection on one phase only points to a joint, damage, or neutral problem there. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.3.3.B.3 and D.3.

question: A 2,500 ft MV run measures 31 ohms end to end on its shield. Under ATS 7.3.3, this shield is:
choices: Acceptable, because 31 ohms is a normal value for a long shield
Acceptable, because the limit is 10 ohms total
Investigated, because shields must read under 1 ohm
explanation: 31 / 2.5 = 12.4 ohms per 1000 ft, which is above the 10 ohms per 1000 ft investigate level. Always normalize to length before judging. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.3.3.B.2 and D.2.

question: A shielded cable fails its VLF withstand, and the crew wants to locate the fault with a thumper. IEEE 400 cautions that:
choices: It can harm sound insulation; use minimum voltage and time
Thumping is harmless to XLPE and can run at full set voltage
Thumping must be done before any withstand test
Thumping is allowed only on paper-insulated cable
explanation: IEEE 400-2023 notes that thumping at high voltage can affect the dielectric properties of the cable system. It recommends minimizing voltage and time and repeating field tests after repair. Fault location itself is covered by IEEE 1234. Source: IEEE 400-2023, 5.5.

question: A splice 15 ft from the termination doesn't show on a TDR trace taken at that termination. The likely reason is:
choices: TDR can't see splices at all
The cable must be energized for TDR
The far-end reflection masks every feature near the test end
It's in the blind spot set by the pulse width
explanation: IEEE 400 notes a blind spot at the injection point whose length depends on pulse width. A narrower pulse shortens it. TDR also needs the cable discharged and will not reveal most insulation defects. Source: IEEE 400-2023, Table 12.
